claims.text: VoiceDebrief turns a voice note or audio file into a transcript, a translation and a debrief in one pass, in the browser, with no account, no upload and nothing to install.
claims.quote: Drop a voice note or an audio file. Get the debrief. One pass, in your browser. No account, no upload to us, nothing to install.

claims.text: A 42-second note costs about a third of a penny on the user's own OpenRouter key.
claims.quote: A 42-second note costs about a third of a penny.

value.unit: seconds of audio for about a third of a penny

claims.text: The WhatsApp number runs through an n8n workflow behind a Cloudflare Worker, the one part of the product with a server, and not the part the article is about.
claims.quote: through an n8n workflow behind a Cloudflare Worker, which is the one part of the product with a server

claims.text: The first commit is on 28 July 2026; the week of 3 August has 127 commits and 10 releases, the week of 10 August 64 commits and 3 releases.
claims.quote: the week of 3 August, 127 commits and 10 releases

value.unit: commits in the week of 3 August 2026

claims.text: The week of 17 August has no commits at all, the week after eleven, then three, and the last commit is on 7 September, a release record.
claims.quote: Then the week of 17 August has no commits at all. The week after, eleven. Then three.

claims.text: The repository holds two hundred and fifty-seven commits and thirty-two tags, and a handbrake you can see from across the room.
claims.quote: Two hundred and fifty-seven commits and thirty-two tags, and a handbrake you can see from across the room.

claims.text: No server is neither a preference nor laziness; it is the product.
claims.quote: It is neither. It is the product.

claims.text: With no server VoiceDebrief never sees the audio, which removes data custody, a breach site, a shared key, key management, billing, a user database, scaling, a single point of failure and on-call.
claims.quote: With no server, we never see the audio.

claims.text: Add a server and every item on that list comes back at once, not gradually; it is a different company with a different cost base and risk register.
claims.quote: Add a server, and every item on that list comes back at once.

claims.text: What stopped the project was not a server; it was the lack of one, because the commercial model needed something the terms would not allow without a backend.
claims.quote: What stopped it was not a server. It was the lack of one.

claims.text: The model was written down on 28 July in a brief headed Billing by not building billing: a payment, a cut kept at that moment, and a key whose credit limit is the user's share.
claims.quote: Billing by not building billing.

claims.text: The minimum top-up is five pounds, because a card fee with a fixed component makes a one-pound purchase return about 59 pence of inference.
claims.quote: a card fee with a fixed component makes a one-pound purchase return about 59 pence of inference

value.unit: pence of inference returned on a one-pound purchase

claims.text: The key model is simpler to build and more profitable per pound than a billing system, because the margin is taken once, up front, and never has to be collected.
claims.quote: the margin is taken once, up front, and never has to be collected

claims.text: OpenRouter's Management API creates keys with a credit limit and lists the use case: SaaS applications that automatically create unique API keys for each customer instance.
claims.quote: Automatically create unique API keys for each customer instance

claims.text: OpenRouter's terms of 31 August 2026 forbid using the service for reselling API access to models, make credits non-transferable, and bar selling or transferring access.
claims.quote: access the Site or Service for purposes of reselling API access to Models or otherwise developing a competing service

claims.text: OpenRouter's enterprise agreement separately licenses making the service available to a customer's own end customers, a door an agreement could open and the standard terms keep shut.
claims.quote: which reads as a door that an agreement could open and the standard terms keep shut

claims.text: Two things matter per provider: can a single key carry a spend ceiling, and may that key be handed to a user who paid VoiceDebrief.
claims.quote: can a single key carry a spend ceiling, and may that key be handed to a user who paid us

claims.text: ElevenLabs keys carry three restrictions, scope, a credit quota as a custom credit limit, and IP allowlisting, and a key stops at its own limit while the account still has credit.
claims.quote: Credit quota: set a custom credit limit to control usage

claims.text: ElevenLabs' Scribe v2 costs $0.22 an hour batch and $0.39 realtime, with four and a half hours free, billed in dollars not credits.
claims.quote: Scribe v2 at $0.22 an hour batch and $0.39 realtime

value.unit: USD per hour of batch transcription

claims.text: ElevenLabs' OEM terms let a business on Scale or above make the service available to its own end users and independently set the subscription price, the closest any provider comes in writing.
claims.quote: Customer will independently establish the subscription price of the Bundled Service for its End Users.

claims.text: ElevenLabs Grants gives twelve months and 33 million characters to companies under 25 people with a monetised use case; characters cannot be exchanged or resold.
claims.quote: Grants, twelve months, 33 million characters, for companies under 25 people with a monetised use case

claims.text: Groq's Whisper large v3 turbo at $0.04 an hour is the cheapest transcription on the list, but its spend limit applies organisation-wide, so there is no cap on a key.
claims.quote: Whisper large v3 turbo at $0.04 an hour, the cheapest transcription on the list

claims.text: Mistral caps spend per workspace, OpenAI per organisation, Deepgram's keys expire but do not meter, and AWS budgets act after the fact; none has a prepaid key with a cap.
claims.quote: Groq, Mistral and OpenAI cap the organisation or the workspace; Deepgram's keys expire but do not meter; AWS budgets act after the fact.

claims.text: A gateway like Portkey is a per-key meter someone else runs, and also a server the audio passes through, which changes the privacy story to a third party we chose sees it.
claims.quote: A gateway is a per-key meter that someone else runs.

claims.text: The two providers whose keys carry a ceiling, OpenRouter and ElevenLabs, are the two whose terms say most about resale, because a capped key is what makes resale easy.
claims.quote: The two providers whose keys carry a ceiling, OpenRouter and ElevenLabs, are the two whose terms say the most about resale

claims.text: Four routes remain: the forbidden capped OpenRouter key, a provider that lets a capped key be issued under its terms, bring your own key as today, and a metering proxy.
claims.quote: What we can do without anyone's permission, today, is keep route 3 and make the key page shorter.

claims.text: A metering proxy is the smallest possible backend and still a backend; it is the last resort and the only route that needs nobody's permission.
claims.quote: It is the last resort, and it is also the only route that needs nobody's permission.

claims.text: The ask to every provider is one sentence: let the credit limit be a property of a key that a user can buy through us, so that we never hold the audio and never run the meter.
claims.quote: let the credit limit be a property of a key that a user can buy through us, so that we never hold the audio and never run the meter

claims.text: For ElevenLabs, apply to Grants with the monetised use case and ask whether a capped key issued under the OEM terms may be given to a paying end user for Scribe only.
claims.quote: Apply to Grants with the monetised use case.

claims.text: Every answer is recorded in the VoiceDebrief repository as an issue with the date, so the map can be updated as a new version rather than a new article.
claims.quote: every answer in the VoiceDebrief repository, as an issue, with the date

claims.text: The terms are read, not interpreted: every clause is quoted from the provider's page on 12 October 2026, none of it is legal advice, and OEM and enterprise terms are to be negotiated.
claims.quote: The terms are read, not interpreted.

claims.text: The owner does not know when OpenRouter's reselling clause arrived; it is in the terms of 31 August 2026 and in a forum thread about six months earlier.
claims.quote: I do not know when OpenRouter's clause arrived.

claims.text: Three providers' terms were not read, AssemblyAI, Groq and Mistral, because their keys cannot be capped; the agents should read them before writing.
claims.quote: Three providers' terms were not read

claims.text: The commit counts show when the work stopped, not why; the why is the owner's account, as someone involved.
claims.quote: They show when the work stopped, not why; the why is my account, as someone involved.

claims.text: Route 2 may not exist: ElevenLabs' OEM terms were written for bundling, not for a key a user buys, and the answer may be no, in which case route 4 follows with the privacy sentence changed.
claims.quote: Route 2 may not exist.
